summary:
Earth Analog Analyzer is a C++17 program I developed to compare five locations on Earth with two regions: Gale Crater on Mars and Lacus Mortis on the Moon.

The main idea is to find out which places on Earth have environmental conditions that overlap with those of the selected regions on Mars and the Moon.

The program compares minimum and maximum values for surface temperature, terrain slope, and local relief. It uses the Intersection over Union (IoU) method to calculate the overlap and give each location a score.

I used data from NASA datasets and scientific studies based on NASA mission measurements. Some measurements are still missing, so the current results are based on temperature only. The scores show range overlap, not the probability that a place is a true planetary analog.

I wanted to build a simple tool that makes these comparisons easier to understand and could be improved later with more complete data.
details:
Earth Analog Analyzer is a C++17 console application that I developed on my own for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

The idea of this project is to compare selected places on Earth with regions on Mars and the Moon, and see how much their environmental measurements overlap. I chose five Earth locations: Atacama, Antarctica, Hawaii, Iceland, and the Sahara.

The project uses three environmental measurements:

  1. Surface temperature (°C).
  2. Terrain slope (degrees).
  3. Elevation range (meters).

The program reads the data from two text files: one for Earth locations and another for the Mars and Moon reference regions. It checks the input values and identifies missing or invalid data before making any comparison.

For each location, the program compares its available ranges separately with Mars and the Moon. It uses Range Coverage and Intersection over Union (IoU) to measure how much the ranges overlap. It then calculates average scores using only the measurements that can actually be compared. Missing values are skipped, not treated as zero.

I also added a 25% coverage threshold as a test setting, and a rule that requires at least two comparable measurements before a location can be ranked. The program also checks whether combining two locations could provide a better result.

One of my main goals was to make the results clear and easy to understand, including showing why some measurements cannot be compared. The current reference files contain temperature data for the selected Mars and Moon regions, while some terrain measurements are still missing. Because of this, the current results are limited and may not be enough to rank all locations.

I developed the project using C++17 and its standard library. I used text files to store the data, and Git and GitHub to manage the code and project files.

This project is an early attempt to explore possible Earth analog locations. Its results are preliminary and do not prove that any Earth location is the same as a region on Mars or the Moon. The project can be improved in the future by adding more complete and carefully checked data.
